---
title: "Week 1 · Introduction. Descriptive statistics"
subtitle: "Population and sample. Description and inference. Univariate data, central tendency and the box plot"
---

Two decks open the programme. Part 1 sets up the vocabulary the whole course
uses: population and sample, sampling designs and their limits, and the
difference between describing a sample and inferring something about a
population. Part 2 turns to describing one variable at a time: the median, the
mean, outliers, weighted averages and the box plot, with worked examples on
nutrient intake, global poverty and the world income distribution.

## Part 1. Introduction

Subtitle: *Population and Sample. Description and Inference.*

**What the deck covers**

-   The population: what it is and why we rarely observe all of it.
-   Sampling: the simple random sample, the law of large numbers in action and
    its limitation, what a simple random sample cannot do, and the stratified,
    cluster and multistage designs that address it.
-   Population and samples by research question.
-   How to conclude about a population from a random sample: descriptive versus
    inferential statistics, the process of statistical inference, and the basics
    of a statistical hypothesis.
-   Goals of the quantitative part of the course.
-   Homework: an example of statistical inference in a research project
    (question, design, two waves of data collection, analysis).
-   Takeaways checklist, key concepts and example exam questions.

## Part 2. Descriptive statistics

Subtitle: *Univariate Data. Central tendency. Box plot.*

| 💻 Source | [`mk68-01-p2-slides.qmd`](https://github.com/EBukin/mk68-2023-24-public/blob/main/materials/mk68-01-p2-slides.qmd) | [`mk68-01-p2-slides.qmd`](https://github.com/EBukin/mk68-2023-24-public/blob/9c5d2e6/materials/mk68-01-p2-slides.qmd) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

**What the deck covers**

-   Univariate data.
-   Central tendency: individuals' nutrient consumption in the DR Congo as the
    running example; describing a distribution; the median; the arithmetic
    mean; extreme and influential observations and how to deal with them; the
    weighted mean, illustrated with the average extreme poverty rate in the
    world; exam problems on central tendency.
-   The box plot: describing a single variable and comparing distributions.
-   The global income distribution: the logarithm transformation and the
    insights it reveals about data complexity and change over time.
-   Comparing distributions of income between regions with box plots.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Why Part 2 has no interactive version

The deck reads `materials/data/poverty-population.csv`, a country-level extract
of extreme poverty rates and population used for the weighted-mean example. CSV
files are excluded from the public repository, so the deck is not in the render
list. The PDFs above are the versions the students received. See the
[README](https://github.com/EBukin/mk68-2023-24-public/#readme) for how to
render it locally once the file is in place.
:::

## Data used

-   📊 [DR Congo nutrition](../data.qmd#nutrition) (`congo-nutrition.rds`) and
    the [world income distribution](../data.qmd#income-distribution)
    (`income-distribution.rds`), both in Part 2.
-   The sampling examples in Part 1 use simulated populations.
